verses.text: Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.
For one believeth that he may eat all things: another, who is weak, eateth herbs.
Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth: for God hath received him.
Who art thou that judgest another man’s servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand.
One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.

He that regardeth the day, regardeth it unto the Lord; and he that regardeth not the day, to the Lord he doth not regard it. He that eateth, eateth to the Lord, for he giveth God thanks; and he that eateth not, to the Lord he eateth not, and giveth God thanks.
For none of us liveth to himself, and no man dieth to himself.
For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord’s.
For to this end Christ both died, and rose, and revived, that he might be Lord both of the dead and living.
But why dost thou judge thy brother? or why dost thou set at nought thy brother? for we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.
For it is written, As I live, saith the Lord, every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess to God.
So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God.
Let us not therefore judge one another any more: but judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother’s way.
I know, and am persuaded by the Lord Jesus, that there is nothing unclean of itself: but to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean.
But if thy brother be grieved with thy meat, now walkest thou not charitably. Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died.
Let not then your good be evil spoken of:
For the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost.
For he that in these things serveth Christ is acceptable to God, and approved of men.
Let us therefore follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another.
For meat destroy not the work of God. All things indeed are pure; but it is evil for that man who eateth with offence.
It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak.
Hast thou faith? have it to thyself before God. Happy is he that condemneth not himself in that thing which he alloweth.
And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin.

summary: Paul turns from doctrine to the table, where a mixed congregation of Jewish and Gentile believers was quietly tearing itself apart over food and calendar. His opening rule is hospitality without interrogation: "Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations." The dispute is named plainly — "one believeth that he may eat all things: another, who is weak, eateth herbs" — and the two parties are given symmetrical corrections, because each has its own characteristic sin: "Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth." The free man is tempted to contempt, the scrupulous man to condemnation, and both are silenced by the same fact: "for God hath received him." Paul presses it with a household image — "Who art thou that judgest another man’s servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth" — and adds a promise that removes the anxiety underneath the judging: "Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand." On the calendar he refuses to legislate, saying only, "Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind," because what matters is the direction of the act rather than its form: the one who keeps the day "regardeth it unto the Lord," and both the eater and the abstainer alike "giveth God thanks." The whole argument is then anchored in Christ's lordship over life and death — "none of us liveth to himself, and no man dieth to himself" — and in a judgment already assigned to another: "we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ," and "every one of us shall give account of himself to God." From that Paul draws the practical turn, replacing one verdict with another: "Let us not therefore judge one another any more: but judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother’s way." He states his own conviction without hedging — "there is nothing unclean of itself" — and immediately limits its use, since "to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean," and a right that wounds has already stopped being love: "if thy brother be grieved with thy meat, now walkest thou not charitably. Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died." The controlling principle is a reordering of what religion is about: "the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost." So the strong are told to "follow after the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another," to grant that "All things indeed are pure" while conceding that "it is evil for that man who eateth with offence," and even to forgo flesh and wine rather than make a brother stumble. The chapter ends by moving the whole question inward to conscience before God: "Hast thou faith? have it to thyself before God. Happy is he that condemneth not himself in that thing which he alloweth" — while the doubter who acts against his own conscience is condemned, "because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin."
takeaways: Paul rebukes both sides with equal force but for different faults — the free are told not to "despise," the scrupulous not to "judge" — which forbids the common move of treating one's own party's temptation as the only real danger in a disputed matter.

The chapter separates two questions that are constantly confused: what is true in itself and what is safe for this person to do. "There is nothing unclean of itself" is stated as fact, yet "to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean" — objective liberty does not license an act performed against one's own conscience.

Liberty is bounded by charity rather than by a longer list of rules. The strong are not told they were wrong about meat; they are told that "if thy brother be grieved with thy meat, now walkest thou not charitably," so the limit on a real right is the good of a brother "for whom Christ died," not a revised verdict about food.

"The kingdom of God is not meat and drink; but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost" gives a working test of proportion: practices are ranked beneath the ends they serve, so a community that fights hardest over its secondary observances has inverted its own faith.

Judgment is not abolished but reassigned. Because "we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ" and each "shall give account of himself to God," the energy spent auditing a brother is redirected into a single permitted verdict — "that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother’s way."

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 8:7-13 — meat commendeth us not to God
crossRefs.why: Paul argues the same case in Corinth over meat offered to idols, granting the knowledge of the strong while insisting that "knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth" and that wounding a weak conscience is a sin "against Christ." Read alongside Romans 14 it shows this is not a local truce but Paul's settled pastoral method for disputable matters.

crossRefs.label: Romans 15:1-7 — we then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak
crossRefs.why: The argument does not end at the chapter break: Paul immediately grounds the duty of the strong in Christ, "for even Christ pleased not himself," and closes with the command to "receive ye one another, as Christ also received us." That makes mutual reception the goal the whole discussion of meats and days was serving.

crossRefs.label: Mark 7:14-23 — there is nothing from without a man, that entering into him can defile him
crossRefs.why: Jesus locates defilement in what proceeds from the heart rather than in what enters the stomach, which is the dominical basis for Paul's confidence that "there is nothing unclean of itself." The Gospel supplies the principle; Romans 14 supplies the charity that governs how a believer may use it in a divided community.

crossRefs.label: Acts 15:19-29 — that we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God
crossRefs.why: The Jerusalem council decides an analogous dispute by refusing to impose the full law on Gentile converts while asking for restraint in a few matters for the sake of common life. It shows the Church exercising in council the same balance Paul urges on individuals here: no new yoke, but real deference where a brother's conscience is at stake.

crossRefs.label: Colossians 2:16-23 — let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday
crossRefs.why: Paul again forbids condemnation over food and festival, warning that self-imposed severities have "a shew of wisdom" yet no power against indulgence of the flesh. It sharpens Romans 14 by showing that scrupulous abstinence can become its own kind of pride rather than a safer path.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 7:1-5 — Judge not, that ye be not judged
crossRefs.why: The Lord's warning that the measure we use will be measured back to us stands behind Paul's "why dost thou judge thy brother?" and his reminder that each "shall give account of himself to God." Both passages relocate scrutiny from the brother's plate to the judge's own standing before God.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes Romans 14 as the charter of adiaphora — genuinely indifferent matters — and not as a dissolution of the Church's authority to bind in disciplinary practice. Paul refuses to legislate here precisely because meats and days are secondary, saying "the kingdom of God is not meat and drink"; but the same apostle elsewhere hands down decisions binding on congregations, and the Jerusalem council settles a comparable dispute by common judgment. On this reading a Church discipline such as a fast or a holy day is not the "doubtful disputations" Paul forbids: it is not offered as a means of justification, it can be dispensed and adjusted, and its purpose is exactly what Paul names — "the things which make for peace, and things wherewith one may edify another." Communal observance and personal liberty are held together, since the individual conscience Paul protects is being formed within a body, not set against it.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read "Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind" as a stronger guard on individual conscience, and many press the chapter as an argument that no ecclesial authority may attach obligation to matters Scripture leaves free. On that reading, binding the conscience in things indifferent risks recreating the very judging and despising Paul forbids, and a required fast or observance moves an indifferent thing out of the realm of liberty by fiat. Both traditions agree that Paul denies these matters any justifying power, that neither eating nor abstaining commends a person to God, and that charity rather than assertion of right is the governing rule; the divergence is over whether the community may nonetheless order such things for the common good, and how far a believer's persuasion is meant to be formed by the Church rather than reached alone.

interpretationNotes.claim: In the Catholic tradition "whatsoever is not of faith is sin" is read primarily as a statement about conscience: a person who acts while doubting whether the act is lawful sins in the acting, because he is willing to risk offending God. The immediate context supports this, since the man in view is one who "doubteth" and yet eats, and Paul has just said that to the man who esteems a thing unclean "to him it is unclean." The tradition therefore holds that conscience must always be obeyed, even when it is mistaken, and at the same time that conscience must be formed — the weak brother is not left permanently weak but is to be received, taught, and strengthened until his judgment matches the truth Paul states, that "there is nothing unclean of itself."

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters affirm the same conscience-bound reading of the verse in context, and many extend it further as a general principle about the necessity of faith for any work to please God — that an act done apart from trust in Christ, however outwardly good, falls short. Some read the chapter as making conscience the final court under Scripture, less amenable to correction by ecclesial teaching. Both traditions agree that a doubting person must not act against his own judgment, that the strong bear responsibility for the weak rather than the reverse, and that the aim is not to leave a conscience in bondage but to bring it to peace before God.
